title: Einstein (1905): Diffusion of a Spherical Particle and One-Axis RMS Displacement
concept_summary: Einstein's 1905 analysis of a small sphere suspended in a stationary liquid gives a diffusion coefficient D that grows with absolute temperature T and falls with the liquid's viscosity and the sphere's radius. For a one-dimensional projection of the random walk, the mean square displacement grows linearly in elapsed time t, so the root-mean-square displacement along one axis grows as the square root of t. This lesson lets you vary T, viscosity eta, radius a, and t, and shows D, the one-axis mean square displacement, and the one-axis RMS displacement.
why_it_matters: The square-root-of-time law is the signature of diffusive spreading: to double the typical one-axis displacement you must wait four times as long. Because D depends on measurable macroscopic quantities (temperature, viscosity, particle size), the relation connects an invisible molecular-kinetic process to quantities an experimenter can actually measure, which is why it is a cornerstone of the molecular-kinetic theory of heat.

explanation_steps.heading: Diffusion coefficient from temperature, viscosity, and radius
explanation_steps.body: Einstein's expression for the diffusion coefficient of a sphere of radius P in a liquid of viscosity coefficient k is D = (R*T/N)/(6*pi*k*P). Here R/N is the gas constant per molecule, i.e. Boltzmann's constant, so D rises in proportion to absolute temperature and falls in inverse proportion to viscosity and to radius. In this lesson we write eta for viscosity and a for radius, and use SI-consistent units: eta in mPa*s, a in micrometres, D in micrometres squared per second.

explanation_steps.heading: Mean square displacement along one axis
explanation_steps.body: For the x-component of the displacement, Einstein's equation (11) states lambda_x = sqrt(mean(x^2)) = sqrt(2*D*t). The quantity under the outer square root is the arithmetic mean of the squared x-displacements, so the mean square displacement is 2*D*t and the one-axis RMS displacement is its square root. At t = 0 both are zero, while D itself remains positive because it does not depend on t.

explanation_steps.heading: Square-root-of-time scaling
explanation_steps.body: Because the RMS displacement is sqrt(2*D*t), quadrupling t doubles the RMS displacement, while quadrupling t multiplies the mean square displacement by four. Likewise, doubling either viscosity or radius halves D, and therefore reduces the RMS displacement at fixed t by a factor of 1/sqrt(2). The mean displacement is proportional to the square root of the time.

visualizations.title: One-axis RMS displacement versus elapsed time t

explorations.change: Set t = 1 s and note the RMS value, then set t = 4 s with T, eta, and a unchanged.
explorations.observe: The RMS displacement doubles while the mean square displacement shown in the computations becomes four times larger.
explorations.why: RMS = sqrt(2*D*t), so multiplying t by four multiplies the square root by two; this is the square-root-of-time law for diffusive spreading.

explorations.change: With t fixed, double eta (for example from 1 to 2 mPa*s), then separately double the radius a (for example from 1 to 2 micrometres).
explorations.observe: D is halved in each case, and the RMS displacement at the same t is reduced by a factor of about 0.707.
explorations.why: D is inversely proportional to both viscosity and radius, and RMS depends on D through a square root, so halving D divides RMS by sqrt(2).

limitations: This is a teaching calculation, not a reproduction of any measurement; all entered values are illustrative examples.
The numerical coefficient 0.01380649 and the decimal value of pi are modern unit-conversion constants, not values fitted by Einstein in 1905.
The line view sweeps t only; it does not simulate a particle trajectory, and the plotted curve is not a path through space.

RMS is not the mean signed displacement, the mean absolute displacement, the total path length, or the three-dimensional RMS displacement; it is the square root of the mean squared displacement along one axis.

The expression assumes a stationary liquid, a spherical particle, and the dilute-suspension regime in which Einstein's derivation applies; it does not model inertia, convection, or interactions between particles.
At t = 0 the model gives MSD = 0 and RMS = 0 while D stays positive; this is a mathematical boundary of the expression, not an experimental protocol.

teaching_simplifications: The working form D = 0.01380649*T/(6*pi*eta*a) uses modern SI unit conversions (1e-3 Pa*s per mPa*s, 1e-6 m per micrometre, 1e12 micrometres^2 per m^2) and the modern exact Boltzmann constant 1.380649e-23 J/K; these numbers are not quoted from the 1905 paper.
The decimal value 3.141592653589793 used for pi is a modern numerical approximation, not a value printed by Einstein.
The notation eta for viscosity and a for radius replaces Einstein's k and P; this is a notational convenience for the lesson.
The computations rms_quad_time and rms_double_eta are derived teaching comparisons, not equations printed in the source.
The line visualization sweeps t from 0 to 60 s using the lesson's unit-converted expression; it is a teaching plot, not a reproduction of an experimental data set.
